newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's disgraced Salinas wants comeback-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's disgraced Salinas wants comeback-analysts.

text.p: Disgraced former Mexican president Carlos Salinas is trying to prepare a return from self-imposed exile to Mexico but his chances of a political comeback are virtually nil, analysts said on Friday.
After keeping almost total silence since he fled the country in March 1995, Salinas thrust himself back into the limelight this week.

In a big, three-part interview splashed across the front pages of the newspaper Reforma, Salinas spoke for the first time about his controversial 1988-94 presidency, defending his record vigorously and declaring his jailed brother Raul innocent of murder charges.
Commentators described the interview as part of a carefully calculated strategy by Salinas to boost his image.

During his presidency, Salinas was hugely popular but his standing collapsed when the Mexican economy fell apart only weeks after he left office and stories of massive corruption started circulating. Most Mexicans now loathe him.

Jose Antonio Crespo, a political analyst at the Centre for Economic Research and Teaching, told Reuters he had been offered money three months ago if he took part in a campaign to clear Salinas's name.
"At the time I didn't take it seriously but looking at what has happened since, now I do," he said. "A lot of people have told me there is a well-financed campaign going on."
Immediate reaction to Salinas's big interview, which was conducted at his home in Ireland, was almost universally negative.

Newspaper columnists laughed at Salinas's claim not to have known Raul was piling up a huge fortune during his administration and scorned the ex-president's assertion that he was victimised because of bold reforms.

"Carlos is the hero of NAFTA and of economic freedom," wrote independent politician Adolfo Aguilar Zinser sarcastically. "While he was president he only tried to do good ... 93 million Mexicans are mistaken, he is the victim."
Opposition politicians were equally angry.

Felipe Calderon, president of the conservative National Action Party (PAN), accused President Ernesto Zedillo's government of "preparing the ground for a judicial exoneration of Carlos Salinas" and his "triumphal return" to Mexico.
There was no immediate comment from the presidency on Salinas's interview or on the opposition accusations.
Political analysts were more sanguine.
They said Salinas was aiming for more modest goals: to improve his standing in Mexico so he could safely return home and to get his brother Raul cleared of murder charges.

Raul was arrested in March 1995 and accused of masterminding the killing the previous year of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, a top ruling party politician, who was also divorced years earlier from the Salinas's sister Adriana.
Raul has always denied the charges, saying he is the victim of political persecution.

Authorities have had great difficulty proving his guilt in court and their case took a major knock when investigators said a key piece of evidence -- a body found in the grounds of Raul's ranch -- may have been planted and witnesses bribed.
Many believe Salinas decided to seize on the confusion surrounding the case against Raul to publish the interview and press for his brother to be released.
Lorenzo Meyer, a well-respected historian and political analyst at the Colegio de Mexico, said Salinas might achieve some of his aims but could not make a political comeback.
"He could recover a bit because his standing right now is zero so any improvement would be a 100 percent improvement," he told Reuters.
"But in Mexico all the ex-presidents have been eliminated politically. No-one has returned -- it's one of the rules of the system ... the life of an ex-president is rather sad."

Crespo recalled that another former Mexican president, Jose Lopez Portillo, had also fled the country in disgrace at the end of his 1976-82 administration but returned after a year in Europe, albeit to a quiet life.
"The same could happen to Salinas but it will be harder for people to change their minds about him," he said. "I don't think he is seeking political influence ... he just wants to improve his image."
